In [[T0]] for Macintosh, if [[T1]] is set to [[T2]] (the default), hot keys aren't highlighted or underlined. If [[T3]] is set to [[T4]] or [[T5]], hot keys are underlined.

 The following example creates the [[T6]] and Cancel buttons with hot keys O and C, respectively:

 [[T7]] 1 [[T8]] mchoice

 @ 2,8 [[T9]] mchoice [[T10]] '* \<[[T11]];\<Cancel'

 [[T12]]

 Disabled Push Buttons

 You can disable a push button so it can't be selected or chosen. Disabled push buttons are shown in disabled colors. To disable a single push button, place two backslashes (\\) before the button's prompt. To disable a set of push buttons, include the [[T13]] keyword.

 The [[T14]] push button is disabled in the following example:

 [[T15]] 1 [[T16]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T17]] mchoice [[T18]] '* \\[[T19]];Cancel'

 [[T20]]

 Default Push Buttons

 A default push button is typically used to exit a data-entry screen, dialog or routine and accept any changes made in the screen, dialog or routine. To create a default push button, place a backslash and an exclamation point (\!) before the push button's prompt.

 The following example specifies the [[T21]] button as the default push button:

 [[T22]] 1 [[T23]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T24]] mchoice [[T25]] '* \![[T26]];Cancel'

 [[T27]]

In [[T0]] for [[T1]]-[[T2]], the default push button is enclosed in double angle brackets to distinguish it from other push buttons. The default push button is automatically chosen when you press Ctrl+Enter or Ctrl+W. You can specify only one default push button for each [[T3]].

 In [[T4]] for Windows, the default push button is surrounded by a thick border. Press Enter, Ctrl+Enter or Ctrl+W to choose the default push button. The [[T5]] setting determines the behavior of default push buttons in [[T6]] for Windows in the following ways:

  If you [[T7]], the behavior of the default push button is the same as the behavior of a default push button in [[T8]] for [[T9]]-[[T10]].

  If you [[T11]], the default push button changes as you move between buttons. The push button specified with \! is the default button when objects besides push buttons are active. When a push button is active, it becomes the default push button.

 In [[T12]] for Macintosh, the default push button is surrounded by a thick border. The [[T13]] setting determines the behavior of default push buttons in [[T14]] for Macintosh in the following ways:

  If you [[T15]], the default push button is always the same and is chosen by pressing Ctrl+Enter.

 If you [[T0]], the default button in a dialog is surrounded by a bold border and is always the same. It is chosen by pressing Enter or Ctrl+Enter. However, pressing Enter when a text editing region is the current control moves the cursor to the next line in the text editing region. In text editing regions, press Ctrl+Enter to chose the default button.

  If you [[T1]], the default button in a dialog is surrounded by a bolder border and is always the same. It is chosen by pressing Enter. However, pressing Enter when a text editing region is the current control moves the cursor to the next line in the text editing region. In text editing regions, press Ctrl+Enter to chose the default button.

 Escape Push Buttons

 An escape push button is automatically chosen when you press the Esc key. An escape button is typically used to exit a data-entry screen, dialog or routine and discard any changes made in the screen, dialog or routine. You can specify only one escape push button for each [[T2]].

In the absence of an escape push button, pressing Esc when editing an @ ... [[T0]] input field ends the editing and restores the original value to the field. If the field has a [[T1]] procedure, the procedure isn't executed. When an escape push button is present, pressing Esc saves the contents of the current @ ... [[T2]] input field contents and executes the [[T3]] procedure.

 To create an escape push button, place a backslash and a question mark (\?) before the push button's prompt.

 The following example specifies the Cancel push button as the escape push button:

 [[T4]] 1 [[T5]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T6]] mchoice [[T7]] '* [[T8]];\?Cancel'

 [[T9]]

 Push Buttons with Combined Characteristics

 You can create a push button with more than one special feature. In the following example, the [[T10]] button is the default button and is assigned O as its hot key character. The Cancel button is the escape button and is assigned C as its hot key character. The hot key designators immediately precede the desired hot key character.

 [[T11]] 1 [[T12]] mchoice

 @ 2, 2 [[T13]] mchoice [[T14]] '* \!\<[[T15]];\?\<Cancel'

 [[T16]] [[T17]] [, [[T18]]]

 The character expression [[T19]] is the name of the font, and the numeric expression [[T20]] is the font size. For example, the following clause can be used to display the push button prompts in 16-point Courier font:

 [[T21]] 'Courier', 16

If you include the [[T0]] clause but omit the font size [[T1]], a 10-point font is used.

 In [[T2]] for Windows, if the font you specify is not available, a font with similar font characteristics is substituted.

 In [[T3]] for Macintosh, if the font you specify is not available, the Chicago font is used.

 In [[T4]] for [[T5]]-[[T6]], the [[T7]] clause is ignored.

 If the [[T8]] clause is omitted and the push buttons are placed in the main [[T9]] window, the main [[T10]] window font is used. If the [[T11]] clause is omitted and the push buttons are placed in a user-defined window, the user-defined window font is used.

 [[T12]] [[T13]]

 In [[T14]] for Windows and [[T15]] for Macintosh, include the [[T16]] clause to specify a font style for the push button prompts. If the font style you specify is not available, a font style with similar characteristics is substituted.

 The font style is specified with [[T17]]. If the [[T18]] clause is omitted, the normal font style is used.

 Character Font Style

 --------- ----------

 B Bold

 E Extend*

 I Italic

 N Normal

 S Shadow

 - Strikeout*

 U Underline

 * The Condense and Extend styles are only available in [[T19]] for Macintosh. The Strikeout style is only available in [[T20]] for Windows.

You can include more than one character to specify a combination of font styles. For example, the following clause specifies Bold Italic:

 [[T0]] '[[T1]]'

 The [[T2]] clause is ignored in [[T3]] for [[T4]]-[[T5]].

 [[T6]] expr

 When you choose a push button, your choice is saved in the memory variable, array element or field you specify. If you specify a memory variable that doesn't exist, it is automatically created and initialized if you include [[T7]]. However, an array element isn't created if you specify an array element in a [[T8]] clause. The [[T9]] clause is ignored if the memory variable already exists or you specify a field.

 -------------------------------

 Note - If the [[T10]] clause isn't included and the memory variable you specify doesn't exist, the error message "Variable not found" appears.

 --------------------------------

 The [[T11]] expression expr determines the type of memory variable created and its initial value. expr must be of numeric or character type. The following are examples of [[T12]] clauses for push buttons:

 @ 2,2 [[T13]] mchoice [[T14]] '* [[T15]];Cancel' [[T16]] '[[T17]]'

 [[T18]]

 @ 2,2 [[T19]] mchoice [[T20]] '* [[T21]];Cancel' [[T22]] 2

 [[T23]] '[[T24]]' [[T25]] button

 @ 2,2 [[T26]] mchoice [[T27]] '* [[T28]];[[T29]]' [[T30]] button

 [[T31]] [[T32]], [[T33]] [, [[T34]]]

The numeric expression [[T0]] specifies the height in rows of the push buttons. In [[T1]] for [[T2]]-[[T3]], a push button is always one line high, so the numeric expression [[T4]] is ignored.

 By default, the width of each individual button is determined by the length of the push button prompt text. The numeric expression [[T5]] specifies the width (in columns) of each push button. A push button will never be sized smaller than its prompt.

 By default, no rows are placed between vertical buttons and a single column is placed between horizontal buttons. The spacing between push buttons is specified with [[T6]]. If you create vertical push buttons, [[T7]] specifies the number of rows between the buttons. If you create horizontal buttons, [[T8]] specifies the number of columns between the buttons.

 In [[T9]] for Windows and [[T10]] for Macintosh, the push button font determines the size of the push buttons. The push button font is specified with the [[T11]] clause. If the [[T12]] clause is omitted, the push buttons use the font of the parent window (the main [[T13]] window or a user-defined window).

 The following example demonstrates how the [[T14]] clause controls the button spacing:

 [[T15]]

 @ 2,2 [[T16]] mchoice [[T17]] '* [[T18]];Cancel' ;

 [[T19]] 1 [[T20]] 2, 10, 1

 @ 2,16 [[T21]] mchoice [[T22]] '* [[T23]];Cancel' ;

 [[T24]] 1 [[T25]] 2, 10, 2

 [[T26]] | [[T27]]

Push buttons by default are enabled when [[T0]] or [[T1]] is issued. You can prevent a set of buttons from being selected when [[T2]] or [[T3]] is issued by including [[T4]].

 Disabled push buttons cannot be selected and are displayed in the disabled colors. To disable individual push buttons instead of the entire set, see "Disabled Push Buttons" earlier in this section. Use [[T5]] to enable a set of disabled push buttons.

 [[T6]] [[T7]]

 The [[T8]] clause character expression [[T9]] appears when a push button is selected. In [[T10]] for [[T11]]-[[T12]], the message is centered by default on the last line of the main [[T13]] window. The message location can be changed with [[T14]].

 In [[T15]] for Windows and [[T16]] for Macintosh, the message is placed in the graphics-based status bar. If the graphics-based status bar has been turned off with [[T17]], the message is placed on the last line of the main [[T18]] window.

 [[T19]] [[T20]] | [[T21]]

 You can include an optional [[T22]] expression [[T23]] or [[T24]] that is evaluated when a push button is chosen. That is, [[T25]] isn't evaluated when you select (move to) a button, but when you actually choose a button by pressing Enter or Spacebar or clicking the button.

Typically, [[T0]] or [[T1]] is a user-defined function ([[T2]]). With a user-defined function you can select, enable or disable other objects, open a Browse window, open another data-entry screen, or move to a new record. [[T3]] can be included in the user-defined function to terminate the [[T4]].

 [[T5]]

 When a logical value is returned to the [[T6]] clause, the logical value is ignored and the push buttons remain the active control. However, you can specify a [[T7]] that returns a logical value to the [[T8]] clause and activates another object.

 [[T9]]

 A [[T10]] clause that includes a numeric expression is used to specify which object is activated after a push button is chosen. Objects are @ ... [[T11]] input fields, check boxes, lists, popups, spinners, text-editing regions and each individual button in a set of push, radio and invisible buttons.

 The expression [[T12]] has one of three effects:

  When [[T13]] = 0, the push button you choose remains the active button.

  When [[T14]] is positive, [[T15]] indicates the number of objects to advance. For example, when the last button in a set of push buttons is selected and [[T16]] returns 1, the next object is activated. If [[T17]] is greater than the number of objects remaining, the [[T18]] is terminated (unless [[T19]] is issued to activate the objects).

 When [[T0]] is negative, [[T1]] indicates the number of objects to move back. For example, when the first button in a set of push buttons is selected and [[T2]] returns -1, the previous object is activated. If [[T3]] moves back past the first object, the [[T4]] is terminated (unless [[T5]] is issued to activate the objects).

 The following is an example of what you can do with a user-defined function. Five buttons are displayed vertically. The button choices are used to position the record pointer. The N option is included so the [[T6]] isn't terminated when you choose a button. When you choose a button, the user-defined function [[T7]] is executed.

 [[T8]] customer

 [[T9]] one [[T10]] 3,5 [[T11]] 18,20 [[T12]] 5

 [[T13]] one

 @ 1,2 [[T14]] mchoice [[T15]] '*[[T16]] Next;Prior;Top;Bottom;Quit';

 [[T17]] 2, 10, 1 [[T18]]() [[T19]] 1

 [[T20]] gorec

 [[T21]] mchoice = 1

 [[T22]]()

 [[T23]] -1

 [[T24]] mchoice = 2

 [[T25]] -1

 [[T26]]()

 [[T27]] mchoice = 3

 [[T28]] mchoice = 4

 [[T29]] mchoice = 5

 [[T30]]

 @ 12,6 [[T31]]([[T32]]([[T33]]))

 [[T34]] [[T35]]

The [[T0]] clause allows or prohibits selection of a set of push buttons based on the logical value of [[T1]], which must evaluate to a logical true ([[T2]]) before the push buttons can be selected. If [[T3]] evaluates to a logical false ([[T4]]), the push buttons cannot be selected and are skipped over if placed between other objects.

 [[T5]] [[T6]] | [[T7]] color pair list

 If you do not include a [[T8]] clause, push button colors are determined by the color scheme for the main [[T9]] window; if push buttons are placed in a user-defined window, the window's color scheme determines the push button colors.

 The colors of push buttons can be specified by including the number of an existing color scheme in the [[T10]] clause or a set of color pairs in the [[T11]] clause.

 A color scheme is a set of 10 predefined color pairs. The color pairs in a color scheme can be changed with [[T12]]. In [[T13]] for [[T14]]-[[T15]], the color pairs in a color scheme can also be changed in the Color Picker.

 A color pair is a set of two letters separated by a forward slash. The first letter specifies the foreground color and the second letter specifies the background color.

 For example, this color pair specifies a red foreground on a white background:

 R/W

 For a list of colors and their corresponding color letters, see [[T16]] Overview or Color Table by Color Pair.

A color pair can also be specified with a set of six [[T0]] (Red Green Blue) color values separated by commas. The first three color values specify the foreground color and the second three color values specify the background color. The color values can range from 0 through 255.

 The R/W color pair in the example above can also be specified with this [[T1]] color pair:

 [[T2]](255,0,0,255,255,255)

 In [[T3]] for Windows and [[T4]] for Macintosh, the [[T5]] clause does not affect the color of push buttons. Only the message color (if the message is not displayed in the status bar) is affected by the [[T6]] clause.

 The following table lists the color pairs and what each color pair in the list controls.

 Color Pair Push Button

 Number Attribute

 ---------- -----------

 5 Message

 6 Selected button prompt - [[T7]] for [[T8]]-[[T9]] only

 7 Hot keys - [[T10]] for [[T11]]-[[T12]] only

 9 Enabled button prompt - [[T13]] for [[T14]]-[[T15]] only

 10 Disabled button prompt - [[T16]] for [[T17]]-[[T18]] only

 The following example creates [[T19]] and Cancel push buttons with the hot keys O and C respectively. In addition, the buttons have the following color characteristics:

  The selected button is shown with a bright white prompt on a blue background (W+/B).

  Hot key characters are shown in red on a blue background (R/B).

  Enabled buttons are shown with a yellow prompt on a blue background ([[T20]]+/B).

 Disabled buttons are shown with a white prompt on a blue background (W/B).

 When you skip a color pair, you must include a comma where the color pair is omitted.

 Here are the commands:

 [[T0]] 1 [[T1]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T2]] mchoice [[T3]] '* \<[[T4]];\<[[T5]];\\[[T6]]';

 [[T7]] ,,,,,W+/B,R/B,,[[T8]]+/B,W/B

 [[T9]]

This variation of @ ... [[T0]] creates push buttons or picture push buttons. A single button or a group of buttons can be created. In [[T1]] for [[T2]]-[[T3]], a push button is shown as a string of text between right and left angle brackets.

If you use the Screen Builder to create your data-entry screens, you might not have to use this command at all. The Screen Builder automatically generates the commands that create push buttons and picture push buttons.

The string of text, often called a prompt, is specified in the [[T4]] or [[T5]] clause. Typically, a push button is used to trigger an action. The triggered action is specified in a [[T6]] clause. A push button is activated by issuing [[T7]] or [[T8]].

You can create picture push buttons in [[T9]] for Windows and [[T10]] for Macintosh. Pictures on buttons replace the push button prompts.

textos.2befcd47-b746-4471-8f2a-0cc447943ebc#319:
The following tables describe activator, navigation, and terminator keys that IntelliSense responds to.
 Activator Keys
| Key | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [[T0]] | Space (" "). Activator key for [[T1]] commands and user-defined language elements. Displays member lists or Tip windows. |
| ( | Opening parenthesis. Activator key for [[T2]] functions and object methods. Displays value lists or Tip windows. |
| [[T3]] | Period (.). Activator key for system variables or objects. Displays member lists of object properties, methods, or events or Tip windows. |
| = | Equal sign. Activator key for properties. Verifies white space between the property and the "=" character. Displays value lists, value editors, for example, font or color pickers, or Tip windows. |
 Navigation Keys
| Key | Description |
| --- | --- |
| a–z, A-Z, 0-9 | Alphanumeric. Navigates matching items in IntelliSense lists until no more matches exist. |
| < | [[T4]]. Positions the cursor one character to the left. Closes the IntelliSense list if the cursor moves out of context, for example, preceding a period. |
| > | [[T5]]. Positions the cursor one character to the right. Closes the IntelliSense list if the cursor moves out of context, for example, following what has been typed. |
| [[T6]] | Moves the cursor one page up in the IntelliSense list. |
| [[T7]] | Moves the cursor one page down in the IntelliSense list. |
| [[T8]] | Inserts a selected item in an IntelliSense list into the code and positions the cursor immediately following the added item. |
 Terminator Keys
| Key | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [[T9]] | Closes the IntelliSense list box. |
| [[T10]] | Closes the IntelliSense list box and positions the cursor at the beginning of the current line. |
| [[T11]], [[T12]], [[T13]], and other non-alphanumeric characters | Closes the IntelliSense list box and positions the cursor at the end of the current line. |

A constant is a named item that retains its value throughout all operations. The value π, or 3.1415926535, is an example of a numeric constant; the letter A is an example of a character constant.

You can create compile-time constants that exist throughout the operation of a [[T0]] application. You can use a constant and know that its value doesn't change during the operation of your application. At design time, you can effect a change throughout an application by changing only the value of a single constant.

A constant can contain any data type value.

For information about defining and undefining constants, see How to: Define a Constant.
